run.title: Desirability, feasibility, viability
run.objective: Test an idea separately on all three of desirability, feasibility, and viability, and name what breaks when one is missing.
explainer: Three areas drawn as a Venn diagram, derived by IDEO Consulting in design thinking and adapted here for product management. Desirability asks whether customers or potential customers actually need the thing. Feasibility asks whether it can be built with the technology available today. Viability asks whether it should be built at all — whether it can turn a profit, or make enough money to support the business. The point of separating them is that passing one check tells you nothing about the other two.

The running example is a digital water bottle: put an edge device on an ordinary bottle and it becomes a hydration device that measures the temperature you drink at, how many times you drink, how much, and at what intervals. Desirability is whether people look at that and say it is worth having, or shrug and say a regular bottle is fine. Feasibility is whether the edge devices, electronics, and firmware actually exist to measure those things. Viability is whether there is money in it once both of those hold.

Each area needs a different skill. Desirability needs design skills, because you are validating empathy with customers and reading their pulse. Feasibility needs engineering skills. Viability needs business skills. The intersections are where the framework earns its keep. Desirability plus feasibility without viability is an unsustainable product: people want it and you can build it, but every new iteration and every new customer costs you more money. Desirability plus viability without engineering capability is the space-travel case — a real want, genuinely profitable, that you cannot build.

worked.setup: A team has validated that customers want the product and has proved the technology can deliver it.
worked.move: Do not proceed on that basis. Run viability as its own check — can this make a profit, or sustain the business?
worked.because: Desirability intersecting feasibility without viability is a named failure in the framework, not an edge case. The product is unsustainable precisely because it works: every additional iteration and every additional customer consumes more money than it returns. Two of three is not two-thirds of a business.

run.stem: Which statement best explains Desirability, feasibility, viability?
options: Desirability, feasibility, viability: Desirability means that the team can actually engineer the product to the quality standard that the market has come to expect of it.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: A feasible and profitable concept does not need demonstrated customer demand, because the economics on paper already justify the decision to build it.

Desirability, feasibility, viability: A product opportunity must be wanted by customers, technically achievable, and economically sustainable; strength in only two dimensions leaves a predictable failure.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Viability is proven whenever users say they like an idea, since stated enthusiasm eventually converts into paid revenue at scale over enough time.

run.title: Jobs to Be Done
run.objective: Separate the job a customer is hiring a product for from the product itself, and read its functional, emotional, and social layers.
explainer: The framework starts from a distinction that is easy to blur. A need is a perceived problem. Value is that problem solved well enough to motivate someone to pay for it and use it repeatedly. Many products fail not because they do not solve the need, but because they do not deliver enough value. Customer need is a problem, a pain, or a job that users want done — which is where Jobs to Be Done takes its name.

The example is a doctor buying a drilling machine and a drilling bit. Taken at face value that is a drill sale. Ask why and it becomes hanging a picture; ask again and it is displaying an MD certificate in her clinic; ask again and it is so that new patients feel comfortable and trust they are seeing a qualified doctor. Three layers stack in one purchase. The functional need is displaying the degree. Underneath sits pride in more than a decade of study. And the social need is the confidence a walk-in patient takes from seeing it on the wall.

Customer value is the perceived benefit relative to the cost of alternatives — benefits minus cost, where cost means money, time, effort, and risk together. In the drill case the cost is a frame and a hole in the wall; the benefit is all three layers at once. That is why need and value come apart so routinely: a product can satisfy the stated need and still lose to an alternative delivering more of the emotional and social job. Uber against pre-Uber taxis and auto rickshaws is the same comparison, where the stated need was only to get from one place to another.

worked.setup: A customer walks in and asks for a drilling bit and a drilling machine.
worked.move: Ask why until the job appears: photos, then a degree certificate, then new patients trusting a qualified doctor.
worked.because: Taking the request at face value scopes you to selling drills. The job actually being hired for is patient trust, and it is functional, emotional, and social at the same time. A competitor who delivers the certificate-on-the-wall outcome without a drill wins the job while never satisfying the stated need.

glossary.plain: Reading a purchase as a job the customer hires the product to do, rather than as a product preference.
The practical task on the surface — here, getting the certificate onto the wall.
How the outcome reads to others: the confidence new patients take from the displayed degree.
Perceived benefit minus cost, where cost includes money, time, effort, and risk.

handoff.connects: That is how to read what a customer is really buying. Module 2 turns to expressing it as value the product can promise.

run.caselet:
A doctor has just finished her residency. She walks into a hardware shop and asks for a drilling bit and a drilling machine.

Ask her what she is hanging, and it turns out to be photos — one photo, really: her MD certificate. Ask why it has to go up on the wall, and the answer moves again. Her patients see it. New ones especially, she says, want to know they are with a qualified doctor. Ten years of her life went into earning it, and she is proud of it.

What she is buying is a drill bit, a frame, and a hole in the wall.
run.stem: Select every need this purchase actually serves.
options: Habitual — the purchase repeats often enough that no decision is taken
Financial — the drill costs less than hiring someone to do it
Functional — the certificate has to go onto the wall
Emotional — pride in more than a decade of study
Social — new patients gain confidence they are seeing a qualified doctor
run.marking: +1 per right option, −1 per wrong, floored at zero.

run.concept: Desirability, feasibility, viability → Jobs to be done
run.caselet: One recommendation must resolve two linked decisions. First: A team can build a device and sell it at a margin, but research shows no meaningful customer problem or willingness to use it. Then: A patient asks for online consultation but mainly needs quick access to a trusted doctor and confidence that the advice is legitimate.
run.stem: Build the reasoning chain. All three steps must agree before the conclusion is secure.

steps.label: Step 1 · Diagnose the first decision
options: Desirability, feasibility, viability: Design around access, trust and reassurance, because the named feature is never the whole job.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Reduce the engineering scope even though feasibility has already been established for this particular build.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Treat desirability as the missing test, since a product survives only where all three checks overlap.
Desirability, feasibility, viability: Call it viable and assume customers will learn to want it once they have seen it working.

steps.label: Step 2 · Apply the second framework
options: Jobs to be done: Assume every telehealth user values exactly the same outcome from the consultation they have booked.
Jobs to be done: Optimise only the video resolution, because that is the feature the customer actually named.
Jobs to be done: Treat desirability as the missing test, since a product survives only where all three checks overlap.
Jobs to be done: Design around access, trust and reassurance, because the named feature is never the whole job.

steps.label: Step 3 · Join the reasoning
steps.prompt: Which final explanation keeps both decisions consistent?
options: Use Jobs to be done for the first decision and Desirability, feasibility, viability for the second; the labels can be swapped without changing the logic.
Use Desirability, feasibility, viability for the first decision and Jobs to be done for the second; neither result replaces the other.
Use Jobs to be done for both decisions; the later issue should determine the earlier diagnosis as well.
Use Desirability, feasibility, viability for both decisions; once the first issue is solved, the second can be treated as the same problem.
